objective: Explain why removing the focus outline harms keyboard users and how :focus-visible restores an indicator.

original.hint: Think about who navigates with Tab rather than a pointer, and what changes for them when the outline goes.
original.question: Why is `outline: none` on `:focus` a problem?
options: It breaks the layout
It removes the only indication a keyboard user has of where they are
It disables the click handler
It is invalid CSS
original.explanation: The focus ring is how someone who is not using a mouse knows what Enter will activate; `outline: none` on `:focus` removes that with nothing in its place, and keyboard navigation becomes guesswork for sighted users. If the default ring clashes with the design, replace it with a visible one — `:focus-visible` shows it for keyboard use and not for mouse clicks. The declaration is valid CSS, and it changes neither layout nor event handlers.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: State that there is no replacement indicator,so outline removal is not universally condemned. Remove the false keyboard-only description of focus-visible.
evidence: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-visible.html

objective: Apply WCAG 1.4.1: never convey status by colour alone; add a word, icon or shape.

original.hint: Imagine the same screen in greyscale, or read aloud. Ask what still tells the user that something went wrong.
original.question: A status is shown by turning text red. What is missing?
options: A larger font
A cue that is not colour — a word, an icon, or a shape
A higher z-index
A transition
original.explanation: Colour alone excludes anyone who cannot distinguish it, disappears in high-contrast modes and on poor screens, and is invisible to a screen reader; WCAG 1.4.1 says colour must not be the only visual means of conveying information. The word "Error" or an icon beside the red does the work for everyone. Font size, z-index and transitions change nothing about whether the meaning is perceivable.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Balance the alternatives and distinguish the visual color criterion from accessible labeling/announcements. Remove the claim that any icon automatically works for everyone.
evidence: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/use-of-color.html

objective: Justify putting an API in front of the database: access rules must be enforced where the user cannot alter them.

original.hint: Consider who is holding the keyboard when the query is composed.
original.question: Your web app needs data from Postgres. Why put an API in front of the database instead of letting the browser query it directly?
options: Because SQL statements are too large to send over HTTP
Because anything the browser sends can be altered, so access rules must be enforced where the user cannot change them
Because a database can serve only one connection at a time
Because JSON parses faster than the database's result format
original.explanation: Code in the browser is under the user's control, so a client-issued query carries no trustworthy identity or limits: authorization, validation and rate limiting must run somewhere the user cannot edit. That is usually your server — or the database itself when row-level security policies decide what each authenticated role may read, which is how Supabase exposes tables to clients safely. Connection limits and payload size are real operational concerns, but they are not the reason for the boundary.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Remove the premise that every safe browser/database architecture requires a custom API and the claim that a client can never carry verifiable identity. Keep authorization authoritative on a trusted server or database.
evidence: https://supabase.com/docs/guides/database/postgres/row-level-security

objective: State what an end-to-end test adds — evidence about the assembled system — and what it costs in speed and diagnostic precision.

original.hint: This is the slowest and least precise test in a suite. Ask what buys it a place anyway.
original.question: What is an end-to-end test buying you that a unit test cannot?
options: A faster signal about which line is wrong
Evidence that the assembled system does the user-visible thing, wiring included
Proof that every branch is reachable
A guarantee that the code has no bugs
original.explanation: End-to-end exercises the real assembly: routing, serialization, storage, rendering. That is its value and also its cost — it is slower and, when it fails, it points at the whole system rather than at a line.

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Replace absolute cannot/slowest/least-precise claims with bounded integration evidence. Keep user-flow coverage distinct from localization,branch coverage and universal correctness.

objective: Recognize an assertion that is too weak to fail: a defined-check accepts every wrong number.

original.hint: Ask how large the set of values is that would satisfy this assertion.
original.question: `discount(price, percent)` should return the reduced price. A test asserts `expect(discount(100, 10)).toBeDefined()`. Which bug does it miss?
options: The function being deleted
Returning any number at all — including the wrong one
The function throwing
A syntax error in the file
original.explanation: The assertion asks whether something came back, not whether it is right: discount(100, 10) returning 1000 satisfies it. A deleted function or a thrown error would still fail the test, because the call itself blows up before the assertion runs — those bugs are covered, the wrong number is not. Name the expected value when one exists: expect(discount(100, 10)).toBe(90).

defects: Correct option was conspicuously longer or more detailed than the alternatives.
rationale: Use one concrete wrong result rather than a conspicuously detailed any-number option. Distinguish mere definedness from the expected numerical answer.
evidence: https://jestjs.io/docs/expect#tobedefined
